Rankings of leader attributes in northern Afghanistan (Bhatia and Monroe 2024)

Source: R/data.R
afghan_leaders.Rd

Respondents of a household survey experiment conducted in 2016-2017 in Balkh, Kunduz and Sar-e Pol provinces ranked six attributes of political leaders from most important (1) to least important (6), after hearing one of four randomly assigned vignettes: none (control), on bribery, on nepotism, or on insecurity (Bhatia and Monroe 2024). One row per respondent and attribute (the long layout of rologit()); 2,479 respondents with a complete ranking.

Usage

data(afghan_leaders)

Format

A data frame with 14,874 rows (2,479 respondents times 6 attributes) and 9 variables:

id

Respondent identifier.

attribute

Factor: religious (strong religious values), educated (well educated), mujahideen (experience as a mujahideen fighter), government (many years of experience in government), military (experience in the Afghan military), honest (personally honest and incorruptible).

rank

1 (most important) to 6 (least important).

treatment

Factor, the randomized vignette: control, bribery, nepotism, insecurity.

female

1 if female (recorded by the enumerator).

age

Age in years.

education

Factor: none, primary, secondary, vocational (post-secondary vocational training), some_university, university, madrassa.

ethnicity

Factor: pashtun, tajik, uzbek, turkmen, hazara, baloch, other.

province

Factor: Balkh, Kunduz, Sar-e Pol.

Source

Bhatia, J. and Monroe, S.L. (2024). Insecurity and support for female leadership in conflict states: Evidence from Afghanistan. British Journal of Political Science, 54, 771-792. doi:10.1017/S000712342300056X

Provenance and terms

From the replication archive of Bhatia and Monroe (2024) at the Harvard Dataverse (doi:10.7910/DVN/OIV11K , version 1.0, released under CC0 1.0): the file Afghan_Data_All_Clean.csv (md5 8c9d3d11d81efdad4ded7770a1dd6e77), with the codes of the deposit's codebook. Kept: the four arms of the vignette experiment (Treatment 1-4), the six attribute rankings Att_Strong_Rel, Att_Well_Ed, Att_Muj, Att_Gov_Exp, Att_Afg_Mil, Att_Hon where they form a complete ranking without ties, and five respondent characteristics; the respondent's village, district and place of birth are not carried over. The rebuilding script is data-raw/make_examples.R of the development repository. The paper analyses the conjoint experiment of the same survey; these rankings are not among its models. In the deposit 1 is the most important, as the codebook defines the question; the paper's code reverses the scale of the importance items it uses (6 the most important).

See also

Other datasets: bes1987, bes2010, cabinets, defection, fluvax, pa2006, pres2004, sanctions

Examples

data(afghan_leaders)
## mean rank of each attribute by vignette
round(tapply(afghan_leaders$rank, afghan_leaders[c("attribute", "treatment")], mean), 2)
#>             treatment
#> attribute    control bribery nepotism insecurity
#>   religious     3.06    3.24     3.14       3.11
#>   educated      2.26    2.14     2.23       2.22
#>   mujahideen    4.80    4.95     4.89       4.82
#>   government    4.15    4.10     4.06       4.15
#>   military      4.51    4.43     4.54       4.53
#>   honest        2.22    2.14     2.14       2.17
m <- rologit(rank ~ 1 | treatment + female + age, data = afghan_leaders, id = "id",
             alt = "attribute", ref = "educated")
summary(m)
#> Rank-ordered logit

## do the first choices follow the same preferences as the later ranks?
rank_test(m, after = 1)
#> Stability of preferences across ranking stages (position 1 against later; 2479 ranking(s) with later stages)
